title: Stability and tie-breaking in online warehouse reoptimisation
shortTitle: Same three trips, different fate: tie-breaking decides warehouse stability
oneLine: Five orders, two bins: plans (1,2,2) and (2,2,1) both take three trips, but a picker who reoptimises as orders arrive and always takes the remainder first is overwhelmed at about 76% of capacity, while filling the cart first is stable to full capacity; the paper also proves the Lorenz–Otto–Gendreau low-rate conjecture.
abstract: A warehouse picker who, whenever new orders arrive, recomputes the fastest way to finish the known orders is said to reoptimise. This candidate answers two questions about that policy for the cart models of Lorenz, Otto and Gendreau (Networks, 2025). First, solving every snapshot exactly does not determine stability. With five identical orders at one shelf and a two-bin cart, the plans (1,2,2) and (2,2,1) both need three trips, so a solver may return either. In the non-interventionist manual-cart model, always taking the remainder first is stable only below the root of E⌈Pois(ρ)/c⌉ = 1, about 76% of capacity with two bins, 49% with eight and tending to 1/e for very large carts, whereas always filling the cart first is stable up to full capacity. The two rules bracket every exact tie rule; the paper gives the exact long-run makespan ratio of remainder first at every load, shows that it approaches but never reaches two, and shows that the gap survives positive picking times (sharply with two bins) and two distinct shelf locations. Breaking ties by total order completion time selects full first. Second, the paper proves the authors' low-rate conjecture for all three of their cart models: if appending each new order on its own costs time B, Poisson arrivals with λE[B] < 1 keep the backlog logarithmic almost surely, with explicit finite-horizon bounds. That condition is deliberately conservative. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Tie-breaking decides stability (Propositions 7–8, Theorem 9, proof): for identical orders at one shelf in Pcart-N with capacity c and ρ arrivals per tour, remainder first is positive recurrent exactly when E⌈Pois(ρ)/c⌉ < 1 (null recurrent at equality), full first is stable for ρ < c, and the two bracket every exact tie rule.

Exact cost (Theorem 9, Theorem 13, proof): the long-run makespan ratio of remainder first is max{1, G_c}/max{1, ρ/c} at every load; it is always below two and approaches two along overloaded sequences.

Where it breaks (Theorem 11, proof with rational root certificates): the remainder-first threshold is about 76% of capacity at c = 2 and 49% at c = 8, and ρ_c/c → 1/e with an explicit logarithmic correction; beyond it the drift can be exponentially small, so short simulations can miss the instability.
A principled repair (Proposition 14, proof): with zero picking time, breaking ties by total order completion time selects full first.

Robustness (Theorems 15–17, proof): the separation survives positive picking time at every c ≥ 2, has a unique sharp threshold at c = 2, and survives two distinct shelf locations, with a proved makespan loss of at least about 10.7% in an explicit instance.

The conjecture (Proposition 1, Theorems 2–5, Corollary 6, proof): for Pcart-N, Pcart and Robot, Poisson arrivals with λE[B] < 1, where B is the cost of appending one order on its own, keep the backlog O(log n) almost surely and the makespan ratio 1 + O(log n / n), for every tie rule, with explicit completion, backlog and delay bounds.

narration: Same three trips, different fate. An Evidence Press briefing on tie-breaking in warehouse order picking. Picture a warehouse worker pushing a cart with two bins. Each customer order fills one bin, and new orders keep arriving. A common rule is to reoptimise: every time the list of orders changes, work out the fastest way to finish everything on it, start that plan, and throw the rest away when new orders arrive. Now suppose five orders are waiting at the same shelf. One plan takes a single order first, then two full cartloads. Another takes two full cartloads first, and the single order last. Both need three trips and finish at exactly the same time, so a solver may return either. But orders keep arriving during the first trip, and the plan is recomputed. The paper shows that this harmless-looking tie decides whether the warehouse keeps up. A picker who always takes the leftover orders first falls further and further behind once demand passes about seventy-six per cent of what the cart can carry. With eight bins that happens at about forty-nine per cent, and for very large carts at about thirty-seven per cent. A picker who always fills the cart first keeps up all the way to full capacity. The gap survives picking times and two separate shelves, and a simple tie-breaking rule, finishing orders as early as possible on average, picks the safe option. The paper also proves an open conjecture from the research that introduced these models: when orders are rare enough, reoptimisation is always stable, whatever the tie rule, although the condition it proves is cautious. The results have written proofs and computer checks, but only synthetic data, not real warehouse records. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on thirty-one October twenty twenty-six, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: In the one-shelf non-interventionist cart model, break ties between makespan-optimal plans by filling the cart first (equivalently, by total order completion time); remainder first is unstable above an explicit threshold. Reoptimisation of any tie rule is stable when λE[B] < 1 in all three cart models.
decisionObject.scope: Identical orders at one shelf (with positive-picking and two-location extensions) for the tie result; Pcart-N, Pcart and Robot with Poisson arrivals for the conjecture. General multi-aisle layouts, interventionist tie rules, several pickers and operating data are not covered.
